stem: On what date was the Rudd Concession signed at Bulawayo?

options.content: 30 October 1888
options.rationale: Correct: Lobengula made his mark on this date.

options.content: 29 October 1889, the date on which the Charter was granted to the Company
options.rationale: This is the date of the Royal Charter.

options.content: 12 September 1890, the day the flag was raised at Fort Salisbury
options.rationale: This is the date of the occupation.

options.content: 11 February 1888
options.rationale: This is the approximate date of the Moffat Treaty.

explanation: The Concession was signed on 30 October 1888; the Charter followed a year later and the flag was raised in 1890.

stem: What did the Rudd Concession give to Rhodes's agents?

options.content: Exclusive rights over metals and minerals in Lobengula's kingdom
options.rationale: Correct: it was a mining concession.

options.content: The ownership of all the land from the Limpopo to the Zambezi
options.rationale: It gave mineral rights, not ownership of the land.

options.content: The right to govern the Ndebele and the Shona on behalf of the Crown
options.rationale: Governing powers came with the Charter.

options.content: The right to build a railway to Bulawayo
options.rationale: A railway was not part of the Concession.

explanation: The Concession gave mineral rights. The right to administer came from the Royal Charter of 1889.

stem: What did Lobengula receive under the Rudd Concession?

options.content: A promise of British soldiers to defend Bulawayo
options.rationale: No such promise was made.

options.content: The title of King of Mashonaland, recognised by the Crown
options.rationale: He received no such title.

options.content: £100 a month, 1,000 rifles with ammunition and a gunboat or £500
options.rationale: Correct: payments in money and arms.

options.content: A farm of 3,000 acres in the Cape Colony for his family
options.rationale: No farm was promised.

explanation: He was promised £100 monthly, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 rounds and a steam gunboat (or £500 instead).

stem: Why did Lobengula send Babayane and Mshete to London in 1889?

options.content: To sign a treaty making Matabeleland a British colony and accept the Queen as his ruler
options.rationale: He did not want to give up his independence.

options.content: To ask Queen Victoria about the Concession and the white men in his country
options.rationale: Correct: he wanted the Queen's help to clarify the Concession.

options.content: To buy guns for the war against the Shona
options.rationale: The purpose was diplomatic, not buying weapons.

options.content: To invite the Pioneer Column to enter Mashonaland on his behalf
options.rationale: He did not invite the column.

explanation: Lobengula wished to find out how far the Queen supported Rhodes's men and to protect his position. The mission did not stop the Charter.
hints: Think about how he tried to check what the Concession meant.

stem: What was the effect of the Royal Charter of 29 October 1889?

options.content: It ended Lobengula's rule over the Ndebele
options.rationale: The Ndebele state continued until 1893-94.

options.content: It gave Rhodes the title of governor of the Cape Colony
options.rationale: He became prime minister of the Cape in 1890, a separate matter.

options.content: It cancelled the Rudd Concession and returned all mineral rights to Lobengula as the king of the Ndebele people
options.rationale: The Concession was used as the basis of the Charter.

options.content: It gave the BSA Company authority to administer and develop the territory north of the Limpopo
options.rationale: Correct: the Company became a ruling body.

explanation: The Charter allowed the Company to make treaties, raise police, hold land and mineral rights and administer, subject to some British control.
hints: Think of what a chartered company could do.

stem: Why did the Pioneer Column enter Mashonaland rather than Matabeleland?

options.content: Because the Shona had asked the column to protect them from the Ndebele and invited it to come
options.rationale: No such invitation existed.

options.content: Because there was no gold in Matabeleland
options.rationale: The Company still hoped for gold there.

options.content: To avoid a fight with the Ndebele
options.rationale: Correct: the Company wished to occupy without war.

options.content: Because the Ndebele had given Mashonaland to the Company by treaty in 1889
options.rationale: No such treaty was made.

explanation: The Company wished to avoid war with the Ndebele, who had a large army, and Mashonaland was less strongly defended. The Concession was used to claim Mashonaland.
hints: Think of the strength of the Ndebele army.

stem: Which statement best explains why the Rudd Concession is still a matter of debate?

options.content: No copy of the document has ever been found
options.rationale: A text survives.

options.content: Lobengula never denied signing it
options.rationale: He did claim he had been misled.

options.content: It was signed by Rhodes himself, who was known to be present at the signing in Bulawayo in October 1888 and to have read it aloud
options.rationale: Rudd, Maguire and Thompson signed for the party.

options.content: The king and the Company understood the transaction differently, and the written text favoured the Company
options.rationale: Correct: the dispute is about meaning and interpretation.

explanation: The key points are how the terms were explained to Lobengula and what he believed he granted, set against the written words.
hints: Think of the interpreter, the king's complaint and the written text.

stem: Which of the following is the best evidence that rivalry with other states influenced the speed of British occupation?

options.content: The Pioneer Column was made up of volunteers who had been recruited directly in Britain and brought out by sea to Beira
options.rationale: The column was recruited from southern Africa.

options.content: Rhodes sent agents to Shona chiefs to make treaties before the Portuguese could claim the east
options.rationale: Correct: treaty-making was a race against rivals.

options.content: The Charter was granted to a company and not to a government department
options.rationale: That shows a method, not a rivalry.

options.content: Lobengula protested against the column's entry into Mashonaland
options.rationale: This shows his reaction, not the influence of rivals.

explanation: Treaty-making with Shona chiefs and the ultimatum to Portugal in January 1890 show that Britain and the Company were acting against competitors.

stem: The Pioneer Column raised the flag at Fort Salisbury on 12 September 1890.
explanation: True. The date is celebrated in settler tradition as Pioneer Day.

stem: The Rudd Concession gave the Company ownership of all the land in Lobengula's kingdom.
explanation: False. It granted exclusive mineral rights and the right to do what was needed to win them. The Company later claimed more.

stem: The Pioneer Column marched through the centre of Matabeleland and fought a battle against the Ndebele army.
explanation: False. The column went round the main Ndebele area to Mashonaland, and there was no battle in 1890.
hints: Think of the route chosen to avoid conflict.

stem: Match each person with his role in the occupation.

right.content: Hunter who guided the Pioneer Column
Missionary who interpreted at the signing
Businessman who sent the party for the Concession and led the Company
Led the party that obtained the Concession at Bulawayo

explanation: These four recur in answers on the occupation.

stem: Match each document or event with what it added to the occupation.

right.content: Authority for the Company to administer the territory
Put settlers and police in Mashonaland and founded Fort Salisbury
Lobengula promised not to deal with other powers without British approval
Exclusive mineral rights in Lobengula's kingdom

explanation: The steps led from a treaty to a concession, from a concession to a charter and from a charter to occupation.
hints: Each step added something to the one before.

stem: Put these events in chronological order.

left.content: The flag is hoisted at Fort Salisbury

explanation: Moffat Treaty (February 1888); Concession (30 October 1888); Charter (29 October 1889); Fort Salisbury (12 September 1890).
hints: The dates are February 1888, October 1888, October 1889 and September 1890.

stem: Choose the correct words.

payload.template: The Royal Charter was granted to the {{blank:a}} Company in {{blank:b}}.

explanation: The British South Africa Company received its Charter on 29 October 1889.

stem: Which Zezuru spirit medium is remembered in Shona oral tradition as having foretold the arrival of the whites?
explanation: **Chaminuka**, according to tradition.

stem: Describe the Pioneer Column of 1890.

points.description: About 180 settlers escorted by about 500 BSA Company police
Led by Frank Johnson with Frederick Selous as guide
Left Bechuanaland in June 1890 and built forts along the way
Reached the site of Harare and raised the flag at Fort Salisbury on 12 September 1890

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The column had about 180 settlers and about 500 BSA Company police. It was led by Frank Johnson, with Frederick Selous as guide, and left Bechuanaland in June 1890, building forts as it went. It reached the site of Harare and raised the flag at Fort Salisbury on 12 September 1890.

explanation: One mark for each feature described.

stem: Explain why Lobengula disputed the Rudd Concession.

points.description: He said that he had been told only a few white men would dig and that they would obey his laws
He claimed that he had been tricked and did not understand that the written text gave exclusive rights to the Company

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Lobengula said that he had been told only a few white men would dig and that they would obey his laws. He claimed he had been tricked, because the written text gave wide, exclusive mineral rights to the Company which he had not understood.

explanation: One mark for each point and one for development.
hints: Think about what he believed he had agreed to.

stem: Explain why the British government granted a Royal Charter to the British South Africa Company.

points.description: It allowed the north to be occupied at little cost to British taxpayers, with the Company paying for administration
It helped Britain to forestall the Portuguese, the Boers and Germany without a direct government commitment

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A chartered company could occupy and administer the north at little cost to British taxpayers, because the Company paid for it. It also let Britain forestall the Portuguese, the Boers and Germany without committing the government directly.

explanation: Credit reasons with development.
hints: Think of cost and of rivals.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a report by a fictional Company agent to a director in London, 1889 (invented for this question)

> The king has set his mark to the paper, and the paper is clear. He may say now that he did not know what he signed, but he signed in the presence of witnesses, and he has taken the rifles and the money. The country is open to us, and we must lose no time before the Portuguese or the Boers are there first.

**Source B** — a letter from a fictional Ndebele councillor to a missionary, 1889 (invented for this question)

> The king was told one thing and the paper says another. He asked for a few men to dig, not for a company to rule. If the Queen is a friend of the king, she will say that the paper is wrong.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What does Source A show about the attitude of the Company towards the Concession?

points.description: That the paper was clear and legally binding / the king had accepted payment
That they were in a hurry because of rivals

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Compare what Sources A and B show about how the Concession was understood.

points.description: Disagree: A says it was clear and accepted, B says the king was told something different from the text
Agree that the king signed and that the question was about what it meant; B suggests the king wanted only a few diggers while A shows the Company wanted open access

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How reliable are these sources as evidence of what the Concession meant?

points.description: A is a private report written at the time but by an interested party who wished to defend the Company's legal position
B reflects the African view but is a letter from a councillor who wished to persuade the missionary and the Queen
Own knowledge: the Concession text gave wide rights, the interpreter was a missionary and the king complained afterwards; both are partly true

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A is a private report written at the time, so it is useful for the Company's attitude, but its author wished to defend the Company's rights and may have stressed the clarity of the paper. Source B reflects the African view, but the councillor wished to persuade the missionary and, through him, the Queen. My own knowledge supports both: the text gave wide exclusive rights, but the king said he had been told something different, and the interpreter was a missionary with British links. Neither is a neutral account, so I must weigh them together.

explanation: Both sources are invented: a Company agent's report and an Ndebele councillor's letter.
hints: For (c), consider who wrote each source and what each wanted.

stem: Assess the importance of the Rudd Concession in the occupation of Zimbabwe.

points.description: It gave the Company a legal claim to the minerals and was used to obtain the Charter
Other factors: Rhodes's ambition and money, rivalry with Portugal and the Boers, the Moffat Treaty, and the Pioneer Column
Limits: the Concession was disputed and the Company needed the Charter and force

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; balance is attempted and a judgement is reached, but it is only partly supported or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The Rudd Concession was important because it gave Rhodes a legal claim to the minerals of Lobengula's kingdom and the basis for the Charter of 1889. But it was not enough on its own. The Moffat Treaty had shut out rivals, Rhodes's money and ambition drove the plan, the fear of Portugal and the Boers made it urgent, and the Pioneer Column put men in the country. The Concession was also disputed, and in the end the Company relied on the Charter and force. I conclude that it was a necessary step and the legal basis of the occupation, but not the only cause.

explanation: Credit explained causes and a supported judgement.
hints: Say what the Concession made possible, then what else was needed.
